events.title: Monmouth Court House, before dawn
events.text: Clinton has halted his army at the court house since the 26th, headquarters in the Covenhoven house, and sends Knyphausen's division and the 1,500-wagon train off for Middletown about four. Washington followed him from Valley Forge with about 14,000 men; Lee's vanguard, some 4,700 with twelve guns, lies at Englishtown, Dickinson's militia out in front at the West Ravine. Hamilton brought Lee Washington's orders between one and two. Cornwallis's division, some 9,500 men, will follow the train up the Middletown road from five and not clear the court house until a quarter past nine. The day will be clear and, by Stone's reckoning, about 96 degrees.

events.title: Lee's advance
events.text: Grayson's detachment forms at daylight and leaves Englishtown about six, once a guide is found; the rest of the vanguard files after it toward Tennent meeting house and the West Ravine. Scott's detachment was ordered to move at five. Lee rides ahead at seven.

events.title: First shots at the bridge
events.text: About eight the Queen's Rangers fire on Dickinson's militia near a bridge over a ravine, which this plan puts at the West Ravine. Grayson comes up in support, and the column halts while Lee sorts out whether the enemy is retreating or advancing. He goes on about a quarter to nine.

events.title: Over the East Morass
events.text: The last British troops leave the court house about a quarter past nine, Erskine's rear guard standing on the Middletown road behind them. Lee's column comes on over the East Morass causeway; about half past nine he goes forward with Wayne, who crosses the morass three-quarters of a mile east of the court house to come at the rear guard. Washington's main body reaches Englishtown at ten.

events.title: The first clash
events.text: Over the East Morass and north toward the Middletown road, Lee comes out of the woods about half past ten to find Wayne already engaged with Erskine's rear guard: Simcoe's Rangers, the 16th Light Dragoons and the 1st Light Infantry, about 1,500 men. The dragoons charge and are shot back. Behind them Clinton has turned Cornwallis's whole division round.

events.title: The retreat over the ravines
events.text: The Guards and Grenadiers come back down the road in two columns, the 3rd Brigade crossing the creek to cut the vanguard off, the 4th behind it, the 5th in reserve, the Hessian grenadiers left as a line to fall back on. Scott pulls back south-west over Spotswood Middle Brook, Maxwell after him, Jackson down from the north brook. Lee, with barely half his vanguard still under his hand, falls back toward a line from Craig's house to Ker's, then gives that up too. By noon he is near Ker's house.

events.title: Washington meets Lee
events.text: Washington's main body, over Englishtown at ten, has Stirling's brigades climbing the Perrine ridge when he rides forward and meets the retreat about a quarter to one, by the park's reckoning here on the Rhea farm: 'whence arises this disorder and confusion?' Lender and Stone find the exchange less harsh than tradition has it. Lee is told to hold the enemy while the line forms. The Guards and Grenadiers crossed the Middle Ravine about half past twelve.

events.title: The hedgerow
events.text: Two battalions and four of Oswald's guns stand on the hill east of the bridge and are pushed back to the hedgerow, a fence, Stewart told the court, 'about fifty yards in front'. Wayne's men fire from the Point of Woods. The grenadiers carry the hedgerow with the bayonet and Monckton, leading the 2nd battalion, is killed; he is the highest-ranking British casualty of the day. The rearguard action lasts about half an hour, and Lee is among the last over the bridge at half past one.

events.title: Perrine Hill: the artillery duel
events.text: Knox's ten guns on the ridge and Clinton's ten in front of the hedgerow fire at each other across 1,200 yards of open ground for two hours. Stirling's four brigades, 2,400 men, hold the ridge with the Pennsylvanians and Scott's men in front of them and Lafayette's reserve behind. The light infantry and the Rangers try the American left over the creek and are held. Men drop from the heat on both sides.

events.title: Molly Pitcher
events.text: A surgeon wrote five days later of a patient's story of a woman at a gun; two veterans told of one decades on, one carrying cartridges and one water; Joseph Plumb Martin's memoir of 1830 has her serving a piece. Mary Ludwig Hays is the name most often given. Lender and Stone conclude that very likely several women helped the gun crews that afternoon, and that the legend is an amalgam. The park's marker of 1992 is at a well near Stirling's artillery line, shown here.

events.title: Combs Hill
events.text: Greene, sent right from Tennent, has brought Woodford's brigade and du Plessis's four guns round by the West Ravine onto Combs Hill, about three by Stone and a quarter to four by Lender and Stone. The guns rake the hedgerow from the flank and the British artillery withdraws out of their reach.

events.title: Wayne at the Parsonage
events.text: At half past four Washington learns the 3rd Brigade is withdrawing and orders an attack. Wayne takes the 3rd Pennsylvania, about 400 men, over the bridge against the grenadiers at the Parsonage and its orchard, is repulsed, and falls back to the Parsonage farm. By five, in Washington's words, the British and Hessians are so spent they can do no more.

events.title: The British withdrawal
events.text: Cilley's picked New England battalion works down from the left under cover of the brook bottom onto the 42nd Foot in the Sutfin orchard, and the Highlanders give way. The battle ends shortly after five. Clinton pulls his units back across the Middle Ravine to the Craig and Ker farms.

events.title: Sunset
events.text: Poor's brigade is sent to probe the British right at seven and is halted by sunset, at 7:31, before making contact. Steuben's four brigades, ordered up from Englishtown at six, reach Tennent as the light goes. The armies rest within a mile of each other, the nearest British at Ker's house. Washington's return gives 69 killed, 161 wounded and 140 missing; Clinton's 65 killed, 170 wounded, 64 missing and 59 dead of fatigue. Stone has nearly half the losses on both sides down to the heat, and the Monmouth County historians count 304 British dead buried on the field.

events.title: In silence
events.text: About eleven, midnight by Washington's report, Clinton files his division off through the court house for Middletown without a drum, and rejoins Knyphausen between eight and nine in the morning. Monckton is buried in the Tennent churchyard. Lee demands a court martial, is tried from 4 July, found guilty on all three charges on 12 August, and suspended for a year.

outcome.result: Drawn: the Americans held the field, Clinton got his army and train to Sandy Hook
losses: 370 by Washington's return: 69 killed, 161 wounded, 140 missing. Lender and Stone think the true figure could have passed 500. The missing are not drawn.

358 by Clinton's return: 65 killed, 59 dead of fatigue, 170 wounded, 64 missing. The Monmouth County Historical Association counts 304 dead buried on the field and puts the loss at 1,134; 256 Germans deserted on the march.
outcome.note: Nearly half the casualties on both sides were from the heat, about 96°F by Stone's reckoning. The last general action in the north, and the longest of the war.

sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Monmouth and Monmouth order of battle (read 23 October 2026), which follow Mark Edward Lender and Garry Wheeler Stone, Fatal Sunday: George Washington, the Monmouth Campaign, and the Politics of Battle (Oklahoma, 2016): the clock times, the strengths and the returns. Fatal Sunday itself and its maps were not consulted.

Proceedings of a General Court-Martial ... for the Trial of Major-General Lee (New York, 1864 reprint of the 1778 record), read in the Internet Archive scan for the testimony of Mercer, Edwards, Lafayette, Wayne, Scott, Grayson, Stewart, Hamilton and the aides: Scott's five o'clock, the halts at the meeting house and the bridge, Wayne's 'five thousand, with twelve pieces of artillery', Stewart's fence 'about fifty yards in front'.

Richard Greenwood, Monmouth Battlefield, National Historic Landmark nomination (National Park Service, 1975): the three ravines, the hedgerow 'from Wemrock Brook almost all the way to Weamaconk Creek' with the parsonage at its north end, the Englishtown road 'slightly to the north of the original', the first clash 'between the east ravine and the road to Middletown', the Craig house '700 yards north of the middle ravine', the battery on Combs Hill.

Garry Wheeler Stone, What really happened at the Battle of Monmouth (1995): the Dividing Brook crossed about half past twelve, ten guns a side, Greene on Combs Hill about three, Cilley against the 42nd, the heat 'would reach 96°F', the withdrawal about eleven. Jim Piecuch's review of Fatal Sunday, Michigan War Studies Review (2017): the British company strengths are inaccurate, the Washington-Lee meeting less harsh than tradition.

Michael Adelberg, Dead and wounded after the Battle of Monmouth, Monmouth County Historical Association: the burials, the wounded left at the court house, the heat deaths. Journal of the American Revolution, 'Did Charles Lee disobey Washington's attack order at Monmouth?' (2024): the 27 June and pre-dawn times, Grayson's 1,500 at daylight, the court martial. American Heritage, 'Monmouth' (August 1976): Washington's report.

Terrain: USGS 3DEP elevation at 10 m, sampled to 22.5 m; Freehold borough and the modern roads are left as the DEM shows them. Anchors from OpenStreetMap (ODbL) and GNIS: Englishtown, Tennent church, the Perrine, Sutfin and Craig houses, the hill points, the park's Molly Pitcher well and its Washington-meets-Lee trail, Veterans Park, the Hall of Records. Sunrise and sunset from the NOAA solar formulae for Freehold, local apparent time.

What is reconstructed: the hedgerow, the Parsonage, the Point of Woods, the 1778 bridge, the Rhea farm and Ker's house are placed from the nomination's prose, within 250 to 500 m, and labelled 'about here'. Wemrock Brook and the Middle Ravine, a branch of it, are traced from the DEM, which puts the ravine on a diagonal from the Craig farm toward the brook rather than north-south; OpenStreetMap's Wemrock Brook points did not match the valley and were not used. Of the two 'east ravines' in the sources, this plan takes the driving tour's East Morass on Weamaconk Creek at Veterans Park, since the vanguard's road and Scott's retreat 'south-west across the Spotswood Middle Brook' both cross it; the nomination's McGellaird's Brook reading would put the retreat north of the road where only Jackson's detachment was. Of the two sites for the meeting with Lee, 700 m apart, this plan takes the park's trail on the Rhea farm over the nomination's plaque at the bridge. Every afternoon clock time is Wikipedia's or inferred; the witnesses gave durations. The two-day prelude, Knyphausen's division, Morgan's riflemen at Richmond Mills and the rejoining on 29 June are off the map. Combs Hill's guns stand on the DEM's summit, 230 m north of the GNIS point. Oswald's twelve guns are drawn as eight with the column and the four that stood with the rearguard. Cilley's battalion is drawn apart from the brigades it was picked from.
